title: How do you generate globally-unique IDs across shards — a DB sequence per shard with non-overlapping ranges, a Snowflake-style ID generator (timestamp + worker-id + sequence), or UUIDv7?
topicTitle: How do you generate globally-unique IDs across shards

s1_definition.profdef: Generating globally-unique IDs across shards means producing identifiers that never collide even though many independent nodes create them in parallel, without a central bottleneck. Three common strategies: a database sequence per shard configured with non-overlapping ranges (for example, each shard increments by N starting at a different offset); a Snowflake-style generator that packs a timestamp, a worker/machine id, and a per-millisecond sequence into a 64-bit integer; and UUIDv7, a 128-bit UUID whose leading bits are a timestamp so the ids are both unique and roughly time-ordered.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has many branches (shards) issuing account reference numbers at the same time, and two branches must never issue the same number. One way is to give each branch a different number block — branch 1 uses numbers ending in 1, branch 2 in 2, and so on — so they can never clash. Another is a smart stamp that combines the current time, the branch's own id, and a counter, guaranteeing uniqueness without any branch phoning head office. A third is a very long random-but-time-sorted code (UUIDv7) that is practically impossible to duplicate and still sorts by creation time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make IDs globally unique without a central bottleneck using per-shard non-overlapping sequence ranges, a Snowflake-style timestamp-plus-worker-plus-counter 64-bit id, or time-ordered UUIDv7.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Generating globally-unique IDs across shards means producing identifiers that never collide even though many independent nodes create them in parallel, without a central bottleneck. Three common strategies: a database sequence per shard configured with non-overlapping ranges (for example, each shard increments by N starting at a different offset); a Snowflake-style generator that packs a timestamp, a worker/machine id, and a per-millisecond sequence into a 64-bit integer; and UUIDv7, a 128-bit UUID whose leading bits are a timestamp so the ids are both unique and roughly time-ordered.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has many branches (shards) issuing account reference numbers at the same time, and two branches must never issue the same number. One way is to give each branch a different number block — branch 1 uses numbers ending in 1, branch 2 in 2, and so on — so they can never clash. Another is a smart stamp that combines the current time, the branch's own id, and a counter, guaranteeing uniqueness without any branch phoning head office. A third is a very long random-but-time-sorted code (UUIDv7) that is practically impossible to duplicate and still sorts by creation time.

**One line to remember:** Make IDs globally unique without a central bottleneck using per-shard non-overlapping sequence ranges, a Snowflake-style timestamp-plus-worker-plus-counter 64-bit id, or time-ordered UUIDv7.

sections.s2_technical:
The first strategy is a sequence per shard with non-overlapping ranges. You configure each shard's sequence so the number spaces can never collide. One scheme is interleaving: with N shards, every sequence increments by N and shard k starts at k, so shard 0 produces 0, N, 2N and shard 1 produces 1, N+1, 2N+1. Another scheme is range partitioning: shard 0 owns ids 1 to a billion, shard 1 owns the next billion, and so on. The upside is simple integer ids and no coordination at insert time; the downside is that adding shards or rebalancing ranges needs planning, and range partitioning can hot-spot the newest range.

The second strategy is a Snowflake-style id: a 64-bit number laid out as a timestamp in the high bits (milliseconds since a custom epoch), then a worker or machine id, then a per-millisecond sequence counter in the low bits. Each node generates ids locally with no network call; uniqueness is guaranteed because no two nodes share a worker id and the per-millisecond counter disambiguates ids created in the same millisecond. The ids are roughly time-sortable because the timestamp leads, which is great for index locality. The costs are that you must assign unique worker ids (often via a coordination service or configuration), you depend on clocks not moving backward (clock skew handling is required), and the per-millisecond counter caps throughput per node per millisecond.

The third strategy is UUIDv7: a 128-bit UUID whose most significant bits encode a Unix-millisecond timestamp, with the rest random. Compared to the old fully-random UUIDv4, v7 is time-ordered, so inserts append near the end of the index instead of scattering everywhere, which avoids the index fragmentation and poor cache locality that random UUIDs cause. You get collision-resistant uniqueness with zero coordination and no worker-id assignment, at the cost of a larger 128-bit key and the storage and index-size overhead that implies.

Choosing between them: per-shard sequences give compact integers and suit systems that already shard cleanly and rarely rebalance. Snowflake suits very high write throughput across many nodes where a compact, time-sortable 64-bit id matters, such as event or message ids. UUIDv7 suits systems that want zero coordination and are comfortable with 128-bit keys, especially when ids may be generated client-side or across heterogeneous services.

The senior nuance is index behaviour: avoid random UUIDv4 as a primary key on large tables because random inserts fragment B-trees and thrash the cache; prefer time-ordered ids (Snowflake or UUIDv7) so inserts stay append-friendly.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India shards its transactions across several nodes, and every node must mint globally unique transaction ids concurrently with no central id server.

Problem 1 — per-shard non-overlapping sequences. We model N shards each incrementing by N from a distinct offset, so their id spaces never overlap.

Problem 2 — Snowflake-style ids. We model a generator packing timestamp, worker id, and a per-millisecond counter into a 64-bit long, generating time-sortable unique ids per node.

Problem 3 — UUIDv7. We model a time-ordered 128-bit id with a millisecond timestamp prefix plus randomness, and note it sorts by creation time.

The code includes a ShardSequence, a SnowflakeGenerator, a UuidV7Generator, and a demo generating ids from multiple shards/workers and checking uniqueness.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
-- Strategy 1: per-shard sequence with non-overlapping interleaved ranges.
-- On shard 0 of 4:  CREATE SEQUENCE txn_seq START 0 INCREMENT 4;   -- 0,4,8,...
-- On shard 1 of 4:  CREATE SEQUENCE txn_seq START 1 INCREMENT 4;   -- 1,5,9,...
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,   -- filled by nextval('txn_seq') or a Snowflake id
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
-- Strategy 3: UUIDv7 primary key (time-ordered 128-bit):
-- CREATE TABLE events (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, payload JSONB);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
idgen:
  total-shards: 4
  this-shard: 1
  worker-id: 7           # unique per node for Snowflake
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four shards generating sequence ids, two Snowflake workers, and a UUIDv7 generator.

Step 1 — Each of the four shards increments by four from its own offset. Shard 0 emits 0, 4, 8; shard 1 emits 1, 5, 9; and so on. Collected together the ids interleave and no two shards ever produce the same number, so uniqueness holds with zero coordination.

Step 2 — Two Snowflake workers with worker ids 7 and 8 generate ids. Each id packs the current millisecond, the worker id, and a per-millisecond counter into a 64-bit long. Because the worker ids differ, two nodes in the same millisecond still produce distinct ids, and because the timestamp leads, the ids sort roughly by creation time.

Step 3 — The UUIDv7 generator produces 128-bit ids whose leading 48 bits are the millisecond timestamp, followed by version bits and randomness. Successive ids are time-ordered, so database inserts append near the end of the index rather than scattering.

Step 4 — All three schemes yield globally unique ids without a central id server; the demo confirms the sequence ids are a unique interleaved set and the Snowflake ids are distinct across workers.

Final output:

```

2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] === Snowflake ids from two workers ===
2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] snowflake ids (time-sortable, unique): [...four distinct 64-bit ids...]
2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] === UUIDv7 ids (time-ordered) ===
2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] uuidv7=018f3c2a-...-7...
2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] uuidv7=018f3c2a-...-7...
2026-10-25 17:42:00 [INFO] uuidv7=018f3c2a-...-7...
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Strategy 1: per-shard sequence (interleaved, increment by N)
    shard0: 0,4,8 ─┐
    shard1: 1,5,9 ─┼─▶ union = globally unique integers (no coordination)
    shard2: 2,6,10─┘
  Strategy 2: Snowflake 64-bit
    [ 41-bit timestamp | 10-bit worker | 12-bit per-ms seq ]  → time-sortable, unique
  Strategy 3: UUIDv7 128-bit
    [ 48-bit ms timestamp | ver | random ]                    → time-ordered, zero coordination
```

```
  ═══ LLD — ID Generators ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy: ShardSequence / Snowflake / UUIDv7 interchange  │
  │  Bit-packing: Snowflake composes fields into one long      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each generator does one thing.                         │
  │  O: new scheme = new generator class, callers unchanged.   │
  │  L: all expose nextId(); interchangeable.                  │

  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
  │ ShardSequence    │ │ SnowflakeGenerator   │ │ UuidV7Generator  │
  │ - totalShards    │ │ - workerId, seq, ms  │ │ - rnd            │
  │ + nextId(): long │ │ + nextId(): long     │ │ + nextId(): UUID │
  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Snowflake) ──
  1. nextId() → read clock ms
  2. same ms? increment 12-bit seq (spin if overflow)
  3. pack (ms<<22)|(worker<<12)|seq → unique time-sortable long
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Generating globally-unique IDs across shards means letting many independent nodes mint identifiers in parallel that never collide, without funnelling every insert through a central id server. I reach for one of three strategies depending on the system. The first is a database sequence per shard with non-overlapping ranges: I either interleave, so with N shards every sequence increments by N and shard k starts at k, or I range-partition, giving each shard its own billion-wide block. This gives compact integer ids and needs no coordination at insert time, but adding shards or rebalancing takes planning and range partitioning can hot-spot the newest block.

The second is a Snowflake-style id, a 64-bit number that packs a millisecond timestamp in the high bits, then a worker or machine id, then a per-millisecond sequence counter. Each node generates ids entirely locally, uniqueness holds because no two nodes share a worker id and the counter disambiguates ids born in the same millisecond, and because the timestamp leads, the ids sort roughly by creation time, which keeps index inserts append-friendly. The costs are assigning unique worker ids, usually through a coordination service, handling clock skew so time never appears to move backward, and a per-millisecond throughput cap per node. The third is UUIDv7, a 128-bit id whose leading bits are a millisecond timestamp with the rest random, so unlike the fully random UUIDv4 it is time-ordered and does not fragment the index, at the cost of a larger key.

In our National Bank of India platform, sharded transactions needed unique ids minted concurrently with no central server, so we used per-shard interleaved sequences for compact integer transaction ids, and for a high-throughput event stream across many nodes we used Snowflake ids because a compact, time-sortable 64-bit id mattered for index locality. The one rule I always stress is to avoid random UUIDv4 as a primary key on large tables, because random inserts fragment the B-tree and thrash the cache; I prefer time-ordered ids like Snowflake or UUIDv7 so inserts stay near the end of the index. The line I remember is that I make ids globally unique without a central bottleneck using per-shard non-overlapping sequence ranges, a Snowflake-style timestamp-plus-worker-plus-counter id, or a time-ordered UUIDv7.
